```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, dpi = 96)
```

Online experiments are the strongest evidence digital marketing research can
produce, and also easy to get wrong: too small to detect the effect of
interest, broken randomisation that nobody checks, many variants and metrics
with no correction, and reports that give a p-value but not the size of the
effect. abfunnel follows the experiment from plan to report so that each of
these steps is done and documented.

```{r}
library(abfunnel)
```

## 1. Plan before you start

A checkout converts at about 4%. We want to detect a 10% relative lift (to
4.4%), with 80% power and a 5% significance level:

```{r}
plan <- af_design(baseline = 0.04, mde = 0.10, daily_traffic = 6000)
plan
```

Smaller effects need far larger samples; testing two variants against the
control divides the significance level between them:

```{r}
af_design(0.04, 0.10, variants = 2)$n_control
af_design(0.04, 0.05)$n_control
```

Write the plan down before the experiment starts. `af_preregistration_template()`
copies a Markdown template with the hypotheses, metrics, sample size, stopping
rule and analysis plan; deposit it on OSF or Zenodo for a time-stamped record.

## 2. Check the randomisation

The demo data are a **synthetic** checkout experiment with three groups and
known effects (see `?experiment_demo`).

```{r}
experiment_demo
af_srm(experiment_demo)
```

A sample ratio mismatch, a difference between the planned and observed
allocation larger than chance allows, means that something in assignment,
tracking or eligibility went wrong. When it happens, stop: the effects
estimated below would not be trustworthy.

```{r}
af_srm(c(control = 50900, variant = 49100))
```

## 3. Estimate the effects

```{r}
res <- af_analyse(experiment_demo)
res
```

For each variant the analysis reports the absolute difference and the relative
lift with their confidence intervals, a test adjusted for the number of
variants and the Bayesian probability of beating the control. For the clear
call to action the estimated lift is about 19%, and its interval contains the
true 15% built into the data. Social proof, whose true effect is about 3%, is
compatible with no effect: an effect that small is below what the sample was
planned to detect.

```{r, fig.height = 2.6}
af_plot_lift(res)
```

## 4. Look inside the funnel

```{r}
f <- af_funnel(funnel_demo)
f[f$arm != "control", c("arm", "step", "from_previous", "diff_from_start")]
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.6}
af_plot_funnel(f)
```

The funnel shows where each change acts: the call to action at the last step,
social proof at the cart.

## 5. Report

```{r, eval = FALSE}
af_report(experiment_demo, "checkout-test.html",
          title = "Checkout call-to-action test",
          hypothesis = "A clearer call to action increases purchases.",
          preregistration = "https://osf.io/xxxxx",
          design = plan, funnel = f)
```

The report is a single HTML file that opens with a plain-language summary,
then the sample ratio check, the effects with intervals, the funnel, the
planned against the achieved sample and the method. Report every variant and
every pre-registered metric, including those that did not move.
